meter.explain: A time signature like 4/4 tells you how beats group in a bar. Top number = beats per bar. Bottom number = which note value counts as one beat (4 = quarter note). 4/4 is the usual pop/rock/house feel: ONE-two-three-four. 3/4 is waltz: ONE-two-three. 6/8 feels like two bigger beats, each split into three.

faq.q1: How do I find a song’s BPM by tapping?
faq.a1: Play the track and tap along. After a few taps, BPM Tap averages the gaps into a live BPM reading. Keep tapping and it settles.
faq.q2: How accurate is tapping for BPM?
faq.a2: With steady tapping for 8–12 beats, most people land within about ±1–2 BPM of the real tempo. Fine for DAW setup, DJ prep, and practice.
faq.a3: No. Everything runs in your browser. History stays on your device.
faq.a4: A BPM counter estimates beats per minute. You tap the beat, and the tool turns average tap gaps into BPM. Listen mode can estimate tempo from your mic without tapping.
faq.q5: Can I open delay or metronome at the same tempo?
faq.a5: Yes. Copy the BPM, use Share link (?bpm=), or jump to Delay / Metronome from the related tools. The tempo can ride along in the URL.
faq.q6: Can I find a song’s BPM with a microphone?
faq.a6: Yes. Open Listen, allow the mic, and play the track nearby. Tempo is estimated in the browser. Nothing uploaded. Confirm with ÷2/×2, the metronome, or refine by tapping.
delay.title: BPM Delay Calculator · Note Durations in ms
delay.description: Turn any BPM into delay and note lengths in milliseconds. Tap to set BPM; you can also paste a tempo from Listen.
delay.h1: BPM delay calculator · note lengths in ms
delay.lead: Tap or set BPM, then copy note lengths in ms. Straight, dotted, triplets.
delay.prose.title: Using delay ms in a DAW
delay.prose.1: Formula: ms per quarter note = 60,000 ÷ BPM. At 120 BPM a quarter is 500 ms; eighths are 250 ms; sixteenths are 125 ms.
delay.prose.2: Common picks: straight 1/8 for rhythmic echoes, dotted 1/8 for the classic slapback, 1/4 triplet for swung spaces. Copy a cell and paste it into your delay plugin’s time field (ms mode).
delay.prose.3: Measure the song by tapping first, check with the metronome, then come back here so the table matches the grid you want. Including after ÷2 / ×2.
delay.faq.q1: How do I convert BPM to milliseconds?
delay.faq.a1: One beat in ms is 60,000 ÷ BPM. At 120 BPM a quarter note is 500 ms; halves, 8ths, and 16ths scale from that. The table shows dotted and triplet lengths too.
delay.faq.q2: What delay time should I use for a slapback or 1/8 note?
delay.faq.a2: Use the 1/8 row for eighth-note echoes, or 1/8 dotted for the classic slapback feel. Tap the song first so the ms values match the track.
delay.faq.q3: Can I tap the beat on this page?
delay.faq.a3: Yes. Tap along with the beat, then copy any cell in the delay table. No signup. Values stay in your browser.
metronome.title: Online Metronome · Accent, Time Signature & Tap BPM
metronome.description: Free browser metronome with downbeat accent and meters (4/4, 3/4, 6/8…). Tap to set BPM or bring a tempo from Listen, then click along.
metronome.lead: Tap to set BPM, pick a meter, hear a stronger click on beat one.
metronome.tips.1: Tap until Stable, then start the click. Don’t chase a moving number while you practice.
metronome.tips.2: Use accented beat one to feel bar lines in odd meters (5/4, 7/8) instead of counting out loud the whole time.
metronome.tips.3: If the click disagrees with the song, try ÷2 / ×2. Half-time and double-time feels are common.
metronome.faq.q1: How do I set the metronome BPM by tapping?
metronome.faq.a1: Tap the pad (or any key) in time with the song or the feel you want. When the reading settles, start the metronome and check against the accented click.
metronome.faq.a2: Common practice meters: 4/4, 3/4, 2/4, 5/4, 6/8, 7/8, 9/8, and 12/8. Beat one is louder/higher than the rest.
metronome.faq.q3: Is this metronome free to use in the browser?
metronome.faq.a3: Yes. No account, no install. Pair it with the tap BPM tool and delay calculator on BPM Tap when you need the rest of the flow.

listen.prose.title: How mic BPM detection works
listen.prose.1: The tool listens for rhythmic energy (especially low-end hits), builds an onset curve, then scores likely tempos with autocorrelation. Same family of ideas as classic beat trackers.
listen.prose.2: Room noise, quiet laptop speakers, and busy mixes can throw any detector. Use headphones only if the track also plays into the room mic; otherwise point at a speaker. Try ÷2 / ×2 when the feel is half-time or double-time.
listen.prose.3: When the number looks right, start the metronome to confirm, copy BPM, or jump to Delay. If the room is too noisy, tapping on the home tool usually works better.
listen.faq.q1: Can I find a song’s BPM with my microphone?
listen.faq.a1: Yes. Allow mic access, play the track nearby, and wait a few seconds for a live estimate. Then confirm with the metronome or refine by tapping.
listen.faq.a2: No. Analysis runs in your browser. BPM Tap does not upload microphone audio.
listen.faq.q3: Why is the BPM sometimes double or half?
listen.faq.a3: Beat trackers often confuse the main beat with half-time or double-time. Use ÷2 / ×2, pick an alternate candidate, or check against the metronome.
listen.faq.a4: Move closer to the speaker, cut room noise, and give it 5–8 seconds. Electronic tracks with a clear kick usually work best.

pulse.h1: Online pulse counter · tap to get your heart rate
pulse.lead: No clock. No counting to sixty. Feel each heartbeat, tap once per beat, and read your BPM in seconds.
pulse.hint: Finger on pulse, other hand on the pad, or any key
pulse.hintTouch: Finger on pulse — tap the pad each beat
pulse.lockedHint: Scroll freely — tap Reset to measure again
pulse.howto.title: How to check your pulse with this tool
pulse.howto.1: Sit or stand still. Find your pulse on the wrist (radial) or neck (carotid) with two fingers. Not the thumb.
pulse.howto.2: Tap the pad once for every heartbeat you feel. Keep the rhythm even.
pulse.howto.3: After several steady taps, copy or save the BPM. No second hand needed.
pulse.rules.title: Rules for measuring pulse
pulse.rules.1: Rest 5 minutes before a resting heart-rate check. Skip talking, caffeine, or recent exercise.
pulse.rules.2: Use light pressure with two fingers. Pressing too hard can change what you feel.
pulse.rules.3: Don’t use the thumb to feel the pulse. It has its own pulse and can confuse the count.
pulse.rules.4: After exercise, wait a moment so the first reading isn’t just movement noise. Then tap steadily.
pulse.rules.5: If beats feel irregular, very fast, very slow, or you feel unwell, stop and seek medical advice. This tool is not a diagnosis.
pulse.zones.title: What BPM roughly means
pulse.zones.lead: These are everyday reference bands, not medical targets. Fitness, age, and medication change what’s typical for you.
pulse.zones.light: Light activity: often higher than resting
pulse.zones.exercise: Exercise: can rise well above 100 BPM depending on intensity
pulse.save.title: Save a reading
pulse.save.empty: Tap a stable BPM, type a name, then Save. Date/time is added automatically.
pulse.disclaimer: This is a simple tap counter, not a medical device. It does not diagnose, treat, or monitor health conditions. For concerns about your heart rate, talk to a clinician.
pulse.footer.privacy: Pulse taps stay on your device. No accounts. Not medical advice.
pulse.faq.q1: How do I check heart rate without a watch?
pulse.faq.a1: Feel each heartbeat at the wrist or neck and tap along. The tool averages the gaps between taps into beats per minute. So you never need to watch a second hand for a full minute.
pulse.faq.q2: Is an online pulse counter medically accurate?
pulse.faq.a2: No. Accuracy depends on how evenly you tap. Use it for a rough personal check only. Not for medical decisions, diagnosis, or treatment.
pulse.faq.q3: What is a typical resting heart rate?
pulse.faq.a3: Many adults rest roughly in the 60–100 BPM range, but “normal” varies by person, fitness, meds, and context. This page does not give medical advice.
pulse.faq.q4: Where should I feel my pulse?
pulse.faq.a4: Common spots are the wrist (thumb-side tendon) and the side of the neck. Use two fingers and light pressure. Skip the thumb.
pulse.faq.q5: Why not just count for 15 seconds and multiply by 4?
pulse.faq.a5: That works if you watch a clock. Tapping skips the clock: each tap marks a beat, and BPM is calculated from the intervals automatically.
pulse.faq.q6: Can I save readings with a name?
pulse.faq.a6: Yes. Enter a name and press Save to store lines like “Alex, 72 BPM” on this device only. Nothing is uploaded.
